rationale:
Quota: 1 long, 3 Shorts, 0 carousels. Everything sits inside the GLP-1 focus and is tirzepatide-first.

Long-form: 3 of the last 7 long videos were search-demand formats (first month 11-13, pen how-to 11-11, Foundayo what-to-expect 11-11), so today can be a broad Lane A topic. The breadth rule says broad questions beat narrow single-symptom long videos (2,980 vs 231 min), so I took the playbook's next broad item, "foods that ease side effects". Nausea, diarrhoea, constipation and heartburn become chapters instead of separate videos. The body rests on settled sources: the Zepbound label, the 2025 joint nutrition advisory and NHS pages. It is not a single-trial deep dive, and the holiday-meal searches (Nov 20–28) give it an evergreen run-up.

Skipped long options:
- Keeping results after stopping repeats the 11-04 Stopping video's SURMOUNT-4 and habits angle within 30 days.
- Months 1–6 overlaps "How Long" (10-20) and First Month (11-13).
- The NAION label change was covered by a Short on 11-10 and is still peaking.
- REDEFINE 4 has no fresh randomized data yet, so it stays a watch item.

Shorts: 2 of the 3 are felt symptoms or practical moments.
- S1 is a pen moment (a drop after the shot). It's off the gut so the day doesn't stack three digestive pieces, and it's in our winning injection/pen Short category.
- S2 is the 13:00 lead. "Tirzepatide not working?" uses the Nature GLP1R-variant paper as evidence inside the Short, not as its topic. It's emerging with low competition.
- S3 is a spin-off of L1 (greasy food), which feeds the long video.

The Exp F lines still apply to S1 (08:00) and S2 (13:00) until the test closes on 11-17. Rejected or caution radar items (the psychiatric case reports, alcohol, pregnancy) were left out of today's slate.

pieces.topic: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro/Zepbound) and food: which eating habits and food choices may ease the common stomach side effects (nausea, diarrhoea, constipation, heartburn and burping), why slower stomach emptying makes meal size, fat and pace matter, and when symptoms mean calling a prescriber
pieces.angle:
Broad Lane A long video (log 'lane: A'; publisher adds it to 'Life on Tirzepatide'). Runs 9–11 min at 14:00 ET. Evergreen, with no date or holiday words.

Opening:
- Sentence 1 names tirzepatide and the viewer's question, then gives a short answer by 15 s: smaller meals, eating slowly, stopping at comfortably full and going easier on greasy food are the habits experts suggest most often.
- Next comes a 'you' scenario: a rich dinner sits like a brick.
- At 15–30 s, give the second concrete payoff: the label's pooled nausea rate per dose vs placebo, plus the label's wording that GI effects happened mostly during dose escalation and decreased over time. Never shorten that timing to 'first weeks'.

Chapters, each named as a searched question:
1. Why does food feel different on tirzepatide? Use the label's delayed-gastric-emptying wording.
2. What to eat when you're nauseous. Credit only what the 2025 ACLM/ASN/OMA/TOS advisory says ('avoiding fatty or high fiber foods during the first few days of treatment', at exactly that scope; smaller, more frequent meals). Bland options and eating slowly are untagged tips.
3. Foods for diarrhoea, and fluids. Sip fluids unless you've been told to limit them. Use the label's dehydration and kidney wording, and tag the NHS dehydration signs to NHS.
4. Foods for constipation. Build fibre up gradually with fluids, and explain why that doesn't conflict with the 'first few days' advice.
5. Heartburn and burping. NHS reflux advice goes in only as NHS prints it. 'Sulfur burps' is called a commonly described symptom, with no cause given.
6. Protein when appetite is low. Include the kidney caveat.
7. When to call. Severe stomach pain that won't go away, with or without vomiting, means stop and call your healthcare provider right away. Signs of dehydration or vomiting you can't keep up with means contact your prescriber. Then: 'For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own.'

Rules:
- All habits are 'recommended', never 'proven on tirzepatide'.
- Give label rates with both arms and name the pooled-trial population. Mounjaro rates only if labelled as type 2 diabetes trials.
- Add the low-blood-sugar caveat for people on insulin or a sulfonylurea.
- No foods called 'bad', no calorie talk, no products, doses or titration.
- Land a payoff before the ~70 s chapter change. Re-hook every 45–75 s. One subscribe ask, after the chapter 2–4 payoff. Start the end ask at about 85%.
- Include 'Not personal advice' and the full prescriber line.
- End with: 'There's a video I'd watch next, linked in the description.'
- Publisher: line-1 ▶ Watch next link to Side Effects.
- Thumbnail: 4 words or fewer that keep the gap, e.g. 'Which Foods Help?', with one calm, labelled tummy character. No body imagery.
pieces.target_keyword: foods to eat on mounjaro for nausea
pieces.why: #3 in the playbook's broad Lane A queue. Broad side-effect questions earn the most (Side Effects has 1,064 min), the narrow-symptom rule turns nausea, constipation, diarrhoea and heartburn into chapters, and holiday-meal searches spike Nov 20–28.

pieces.topic: A drop of liquid or blood at the injection spot after a tirzepatide pen shot: what the Instructions for Use say it means, and when to call

pieces.topic: Tirzepatide not working as well for you as for others? Why weight-loss responses differ: the SURMOUNT-1 spread, lower average loss with type 2 diabetes, and the Nature GLP1R-variant finding
pieces.angle: Tirzepatide working less for you than for others? Responses really do differ. Use SURMOUNT-1's spread around the average, with the placebo arm and full population (adults with obesity, or overweight plus at least one weight-related condition, without diabetes, 72 weeks), and SURMOUNT-2's lower average loss in adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes, labelled as a separate trial. For the new fact, use the Nature (8 Apr 2026) genetic study of about 28,000 people with self-reported data: a common GLP1R gene variant was linked to slightly more weight loss on both semaglutide and tirzepatide, about 0.76 kg per copy. Frame it as association research that may help explain part of the variation, with no clinical test available and no implication of drug choice. Drop the rare-variant semaglutide-vs-tirzepatide finding, or if kept, cite it correctly as Nature Metabolism, state that tirzepatide response was near-normal in carriers, and never imply switching. Close with 'averages, not predictions' and a question for your prescriber about your own progress, then the don't-switch/stop line, the Exp F line, 'Not personal advice', the prescriber line and the closing line.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide Not Working? Why Results Differ #shorts
pieces.why: The Nature paper (13 Nov) adds a fresh tirzepatide-first hook to a high-volume evergreen search. Competition is low, and creators have barely covered it. | fact-check: Source error in the brief. The rare-variant finding ('Rare GLP1R variants attenuate weight loss with semaglutide but not tirzepatide') is in Nature Metabolism (nature.com/articles/s42255-026-01656-z), not 'Nature, Nov 2026'. Search reports put it at about 13,725 treated adults, damaging variants in about 0.2%, and carriers losing roughly a quarter of the usual weight on semaglutide but near-normal amounts on tirzepatide. Its page sits behind a login, so the date and figures need confirming via PubMed or another accessible source. The separate Nature paper (8 Apr 2026, s41586-026-10330-z, 23andMe Research Institute, 27,885 people, self-reported data) found a common GLP1R variant (rs10305420) linked to about 0.76 kg more weight loss per copy on both semaglutide and tirzepatide, and GIPR variants linked to nausea and vomiting on tirzepatide. The rare-variant result can't explain why tirzepatide works less for someone, because tirzepatide response was near-normal in carriers. Using it in a 'tirzepatide not working?' Short implicitly promotes switching drugs and confuses the scope. SURMOUNT-1 and SURMOUNT-2 figures are fine if both arms, populations and the 72-week timeframe are given, and the trials stay labelled as separate.

pieces.topic: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro/Zepbound) serious warnings explained from the US label: the boxed thyroid C-cell tumour warning and who shouldn't use it (personal or family history of MTC or MEN 2), pancreatitis, gallbladder problems, low blood sugar with insulin or a sulfonylurea, kidney injury from fluid loss, severe allergic reactions, diabetic retinopathy (Mounjaro, type 2 diabetes), aspiration risk around anaesthesia, and the FDA's Nov 9, 2026 class-wide NAION eye warning, with how rare each one is
pieces.angle: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro/Zepbound) label warnings explained: what each one means, which signs need action, and how rare each one is where the label (or the FDA, for NAION) gives a rate. Use the current Zepbound PI (rev. 28 Aug 2026), the Mounjaro PI (rev. 27 Aug 2026) and the Medication Guide, each with its own URL. For NAION, use the FDA Drug Safety Communication of 9 Nov 2026 unless the PI fetched on publish day prints it. Keep the opening, the 15 s short answer and the second payoff as planned. Changes: (a) Thyroid chapter: in label wording, thyroid C-cell tumours were seen in rats and it is unknown whether tirzepatide causes them in humans, including MTC. Contraindicated with a personal or family history of MTC or MEN 2. Give no human rate. (b) Kidney injury, serious allergic reactions and aspiration: say these come from post-marketing reports and the label gives no trial rate. Keep 'post-marketing' and the label's scope: acute kidney injury in the setting of fluid loss from nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea. (c) Pancreatitis, gallbladder, low blood sugar and retinopathy: use a rate only if it is printed with both arms and the exact trial population. Zepbound pooled = adults with obesity, or overweight plus at least one weight-related condition. Mounjaro = type 2 diabetes trials. Never mix the two labels. Retinopathy is Mounjaro, type 2 diabetes only. Low blood sugar: higher risk with insulin or a sulfonylurea. (d) NAION: 'the FDA says there's a potential increased risk across GLP-1 medicines'. Pooled 126 trials: 6.4 vs 3.8 cases per 100,000 person-years, GLP-1 medicines vs comparators, based on a small number of events. It wasn't shown for tirzepatide on its own, so never say 'causes'. Use the FDA's sign wording: sudden, often painless vision loss in one eye. Action: contact a healthcare professional right away, or your local urgent care or emergency number. Don't mention the providers' 'consider discontinuing' guidance as viewer advice. (e) Add one line saying the label lists other warnings too (severe GI disease, heart rate increase, mood changes and suicidal thoughts) and that the full list is in the Medication Guide. If mood or suicidal thoughts are mentioned, keep it calm, tell viewers to contact a healthcare provider right away, and give crisis resources for the US, UK, Canada and Australia, with no method detail. (f) Aspiration: the only action is 'tell your surgical and anaesthesia team that you take it'. Keep the scoped don't-stop line after the emergency signs, one GI line, 'Not personal advice' and the full prescriber line, spoken and on screen. No dosing, titration, skipping or switching. Don't call NAION 'new' or 'this week'. Title: 'Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) Serious Risks: How Rare?'. Thumbnail: 'HOW RARE?' with a carton and an unfolded leaflet, one calm labelled character, no body imagery.
pieces.trend_stage: rising (FDA NAION label-change hook) on an evergreen label base
pieces.why: Broad, steadily searched worry ('mounjaro thyroid cancer', 'zepbound warnings') with a peaking label-change hook, and almost all of it can be checked against the FDA label, so it should clear fact-check first time and keep earning search views. | fact-check: Good topic. It's a broad, searched label explainer in Lane A and doesn't break any ban, and the plan already handles the safety framing well. I checked the time-sensitive part. The FDA did issue a class-wide NAION Drug Safety Communication on 9 Nov 2026, requiring a Warnings and Precautions update for all GLP-1 RA medicines, including Mounjaro and Zepbound. The pooled FDA analysis covered 126 trials, 134,253 patients (78,217 on a GLP-1 RA, 56,036 on a comparator) and 288,879 patient-years. NAION rates were 6.4 per 100,000 person-years on GLP-1 RAs vs 3.8 on comparators, from 15 probable events: 10 on GLP-1 RAs, 5 on placebo and none on active comparators. Sources: Healio 2026-11-09, Ophthalmology Times, Optometry Times, Pharmacy Times, CNN 2026-11-09. Six changes are needed. (1) Use the exact printed figures, '6.4 vs 3.8 per 100,000 person-years', not 'about 6 vs 4'. The FDA calls it a 'potential increased risk', so don't say tirzepatide causes NAION or that this was shown for tirzepatide specifically. These are pooled class data from very few events. The DSC tells providers to 'consider discontinuing' if NAION develops. That is clinician guidance and must not become viewer advice to stop. (2) The angle promises 'how rare each one is', but several warnings have no rate on the label. The thyroid C-cell tumour finding comes from rats and the human risk is unknown. Acute kidney injury and serious hypersensitivity reactions come from post-marketing reports. Aspiration comes from rare post-marketing reports. For these, say there's no trial rate on the label. Don't invent a rate or call one 'rare' unless the label does. (3) The title says 'Serious Risks', but the Zepbound label also lists severe GI disease, heart rate increase and suicidal behaviour and ideation. Don't present the 8 chapters as the complete list. Add a line that the full list is in the Medication Guide. If suicidal ideation is mentioned, it needs a calm, neutral line and crisis resources for all four markets, with no method detail. (4) Only use a rate if it is printed with both arms and the population. For the Zepbound pooled trials, name the population exactly: adults with obesity, or overweight plus at least one weight-related condition. Study 1 excluded type 2 diabetes. The Mounjaro rates come from type 2 diabetes trials. Never combine numbers from the two labels. (5) Credit NAION to the FDA DSC with its date, unless the PI fetched on publish day prints it. Don't call it 'new' or 'this week', because the piece is evergreen. (6) The working title 'Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) Serious Risks: How Rare?' is fine, because the video answers the question. The thumbnail 'HOW RARE?' is fine.

pieces.topic: How tirzepatide (Mounjaro/Zepbound) works in the body: the body's own GLP-1 and GIP hormones (the 'incretin' effect), what it means that one molecule acts on both receptors, how it affects insulin and blood sugar, appetite and food intake, and stomach emptying, why it lasts long enough for once-weekly use, and what is still unknown (especially GIP's role)
pieces.angle:
Lane A, broad searched question (log 'lane: A'; add to 'Life on Tirzepatide' and the How GLP-1 Works playlist). 9–11 min, 14:00 ET, evergreen, with no news peg and no date words.

**Opening**
- Sentence 1 names tirzepatide and asks the viewer's question.
- By 15 s, the short answer in label wording: it activates the receptors for two gut hormones, GIP and GLP-1. That lowers blood sugar by boosting insulin when glucose is high, reduces appetite and food intake, and delays gastric emptying.
- Then a 'you' scenario: you notice you're full sooner and you wonder what's actually going on.
- At 15–30 s, the second concrete payoff: the SURMOUNT-1 72-week average weight change for each dose arm vs placebo, with per-arm n. Population: adults with obesity, or overweight plus at least one weight-related condition, without diabetes. Copied exactly from NEJM 2022, with the measure named in plain words. Averages, not predictions.

**Chapters, named as searched questions**
1. What is GLP-1? The natural gut hormone released after eating, and the incretin effect. Use a peer-reviewed physiology review. Say the body's own GLP-1 is broken down within minutes, using only the review's exact wording.
2. What is GIP, and why target both? Label 12.1 says tirzepatide binds both receptors. Say plainly that scientists still debate how much GIP adds. Label any animal finding 'in mice' or 'in rats'.
3. How does it lower blood sugar? Glucose-dependent insulin release and lower glucagon, in label wording. Low blood sugar risk is higher with insulin or a sulfonylurea. Mounjaro and SURPASS facts are labelled as type 2 diabetes.
4. Why do you feel less hungry? Use human energy-intake data from a named randomized study, with its exact population (e.g. Heise 2023 Diabetes Care, type 2 diabetes). Brain findings are labelled by species.
5. Why does food sit longer? Delayed gastric emptying in label wording, including that the effect is largest after the first dose and diminishes over time. Never use it as the cause of an effect: no 'so' and no 'that's why'.
6. Why only once a week? Albumin binding and a long half-life, in label 12.3 wording only. No dose amounts.
7. What does the mechanism mean for side effects? One GI line, then label wording that GI effects happened mostly during dose escalation and decreased over time. Then the questions to ask your prescriber.

**Rules**
- Land a payoff before the ~70 s chapter change, and open chapter 2 with a question.
- Re-hook every 45–75 s.
- One subscribe ask, right after the chapter 4 payoff. Start the end ask at about 85%.
- No dosing, titration or switching.
- Spoken and on screen: 'Don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own', 'Not personal advice' and the full prescriber line.
- Ending: 'There's a video I'd watch next, linked in the description.' The publisher puts a ▶ Watch next link to Side Effects on line 1.

**Sources:** Zepbound PI (rev. 28 Aug 2026), Mounjaro PI (rev. 27 Aug 2026), NEJM 2022 SURMOUNT-1, and one PubMed incretin review. No Medication Guide quotes.

**Thumbnail:** 'TWO HORMONES?' with one large pen and a calm labelled gut character. No body imagery.
pieces.why: A broad, high-volume tirzepatide question that no live video answers. Settled label and peer-reviewed sources make it easy to verify, it doesn't overlap the dropped L1/L2 or today's Shorts, and it opens the How GLP-1 Works pillar.
